solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Bouncer‘s nasty whiff caught by page in grand, formal dance (4-4,4)

indicatorNotes.caught by: the whiff is held right beside the page-in-grand group, so the pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: a pong is a bad smell
a ball is a formal dance

annotation.surface: A nightclub doorman with body odour turns up at a grand society ball.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bouncer' looks like the doorman of the surface, but here it is anything that bounces. The pieces spell PING, PONG and BALL; PONG is British slang for a stink.
annotation.definitionFit: A ping-pong ball is about the bounciest thing on any table.

entries.clue: Idiot put in some butter with a sauce (7)

indicatorNotes.put in: the idiot is placed inside the butter

blocks.note: a pat of butter is a small portion

annotation.surface: A fool is making a buttery sauce and getting it all wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Some butter' tempts you to hunt for hidden letters in 'butter'; the phrase is a quantity, the small slab served with bread.
annotation.definitionFit: Passata is sieved tomato sauce, a staple of Italian cooking.

entries.clue: Imminent, time period after dusk (5)

annotation.surface: Nightfall is approaching.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition runs on from 'time', so 'time period' looks like one phrase; split it after 'time'.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: dusk is the last light, and the dark hours that follow it are the night.

entries.clue: Piece placed on upper edge for game (9)

indicatorNotes.placed on: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second

blocks.note: a ridge is the top edge of a roof or hill

annotation.surface: Someone places a board-game piece along the top edge of the board.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like a board game after 'Piece', but here it is game birds, shot for sport and food.
annotation.definitionFit: Game here is the collective word for birds shot for sport and food, and this plump bird is a prime example.

entries.clue: Twelve, number going both ways (4)

indicatorNotes.going both ways: the number is written forwards, then backwards

annotation.surface: Something numbered twelve can be read in either direction.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer is itself a palindrome, which is what 'going both ways' hints at.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by clock time: the hour of twelve in the middle of the day.

entries.clue: Fish filling fishy table – a sell-out? (8)

indicatorNotes.filling: the fish goes inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.fishy: something fishy is suspect, out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a ray is a flat fish

annotation.surface: A fish dish laid out on a table sells out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fish' and 'fishy' sit side by side to look like one theme; the first is the letters, the second the signal to mix TABLE.
annotation.definitionFit: A betrayal is a sell-out, giving someone up for your own gain.

entries.clue: Bones left after hauling up rope (5)

indicatorNotes.after: 'after' means following in sequence, so the letter for left is written behind the bones, not in front
indicatorNotes.hauling up: in a down clue, pulled upwards means read bottom to top

blocks.note: ossa is Latin for bones, familiar from anatomy

annotation.surface: Skeletal remains are found once a rope has been hauled up, as from a well.
annotation.walkthrough: OSSA then L gives OSSAL; hauled up in the down entry it becomes LASSO.
annotation.definitionFit: A specific kind of rope: the cowboy's loop with a running noose, thrown to catch cattle.

entries.clue: Male, great as gyrating – Elvis, say? (8)

indicatorNotes.gyrating: spinning round, so the letters are mixed

annotation.surface: A man as great as Elvis gyrating his hips on stage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gyrating' is lifted straight from Elvis's famous hip moves, so the indicator belongs to the scene too.
annotation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley is the example of a megastar, hence 'say' and the question mark.

entries.clue: Maroon thread (6)

blocks.note: the verb: to leave someone stuck, as on a desert island

annotation.surface: A dark red thread.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like the colour of the thread, but it is the verb: to leave someone stranded.
annotation.definitionFit: Strand is both a single thread and to leave stuck somewhere.

entries.clue: Make light of frost, in America? (9)

blocks.note: to present something unpleasant as less bad than it is
Americans frost a cake where the British ice it: coat it in sugar

annotation.surface: Someone shrugs off a frost in America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Frost' reads as weather, but it is the American word for icing a cake.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are one image: a layer of sugar on a cake, and a sweetening layer over bad news.

entries.clue: Swimmer was malodorous (5)

blocks.note: a swimmer is a fish, here a small silvery one

annotation.surface: A swimmer was smelly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swimmer' is a crossword way of saying fish; SMELT as a past tense is the British spelling of smelled.
annotation.definitionFit: The smelt is a small silvery fish, and something that smelt had a smell.

entries.clue: Sweet, or where “weet” is in it? (6)

blocks.note: in Britain a sweet is the dessert course
'it' is the word Sweet; ask where its last four letters sit relative to its first

annotation.walkthrough: In 'Sweet', WEET comes AFTER S. Afters is homely British slang for the dessert course.
annotation.definitionFit: Afters is the course that comes after the main one: the sweet.

entries.clue: View from neither parent? (8)

blocks.note: the 'nor a' of 'neither this nor a that'

annotation.surface: An opinion that belongs to neither mum nor dad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Neither parent' unpacks as '(neither) PA NOR A MA', with the one word 'parent' supplying both parents; the phrasing is loose, which the question mark admits.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a wide, sweeping view of a landscape.

entries.clue: Savage raced past a gallery (6)

indicatorNotes.Savage: savaged letters are torn up and rearranged
indicatorNotes.past: A joins the fodder, beside RACED

blocks.note: the word itself, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: A wild animal rushes by an art gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Savage' looks like an adjective describing the racer, but it is the verb that tears up the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An arcade is a covered walkway or passage lined with shops, a gallery.

entries.clue: Delightful, blacken name of dynasty (8)

blocks.note: to char is to scorch black
the Ming dynasty ruled China 1368 to 1644

annotation.surface: Someone smears the good name of a delightful royal family.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blacken name' reads as smearing a reputation; it is two pieces: burn black, and a Chinese dynasty.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe someone or something that pleases.

entries.clue: Worried about companion under cover (8)

indicatorNotes.about: the worrying goes around the companion

blocks.note: a pet is an animal companion

annotation.surface: Someone is anxious about a friend who is working undercover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Under cover' sounds like spying; here it is a floor with a carpet laid over it.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: a floor with a rug laid wall to wall is literally under cover.

entries.clue: Woman looking to help transpose dances (9)

indicatorNotes.dances: the letters of TRANSPOSE move about

annotation.surface: A woman who wants to help rearranges some dances.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Transpose' itself means move around, so it looks like the indicator; it is the fodder, and 'dances' is the signal.
annotation.definitionFit: A patroness is a woman who supports and helps a cause or artist.

entries.clue: Fuel smell arising underneath jumper! (8)

indicatorNotes.arising: going up in a down clue, so read backwards
indicatorNotes.underneath: in a down entry this piece sits below the jumper

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, who jumps from planes
niff is British slang for a bad smell

annotation.surface: A whiff of fuel rises from under someone's sweater.
annotation.walkthrough: A jumper is a British sweater, which is the surface's picture, but here it is a parachutist.
annotation.definitionFit: Paraffin is the British name for kerosene, a fuel.

entries.clue: Bowler on head of some long-distance traveller (8)

indicatorNotes.on: the bowler goes next to the S
indicatorNotes.head of: the head is the top or front of something, so the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: in cricket a paceman is a fast bowler

annotation.surface: A bowler hat sits on a traveller's head.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bowler on head' paints a hat, but the bowler is a cricketer who bowls fast.
annotation.definitionFit: A spaceman travels further than anyone.

entries.clue: Additional moment (6)

blocks.note: another one, as in a further helping
a very short time, as in 'just a moment'

annotation.surface: An extra moment.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, extra time, but the two words each define the answer separately.
annotation.definitionFit: Second means another, and also a very short time.

entries.clue: Deprive poor servant losing pension ultimately (6)

indicatorNotes.poor: the servant is in a bad state, so its letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.losing: what is lost is no longer there, so that letter comes out of the servant
indicatorNotes.ultimately: 'ultimately' means in the end, so it points at the final letter of the word before it

blocks.note: last letter of 'pension', removed from SERVANT

annotation.surface: An employer robs a poor servant of their pension.
annotation.walkthrough: SERVANT without its N leaves SERVAT, which rearranges to the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To starve someone is to deprive them of food, or of anything needed.

entries.clue: Always hundred and eleven in blue? (7)

annotation.surface: Someone is always sad at a hundred and eleven.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In blue' seems to mean sad; Everton is an English football club in Liverpool that plays in blue, and a football team is an eleven.
annotation.definitionFit: Everton fields an eleven in blue shirts, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Entertainer in show, and I cracked up (8)

indicatorNotes.cracked up: broken apart, so AND I is rearranged

blocks.note: to show up is to come

annotation.surface: A performer in a show says the act made them burst out laughing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cracked up' is what an audience does at a comedian, which is why it sits so well; here it breaks up AND I.
annotation.definitionFit: A comedian is an entertainer who tells jokes.

entries.clue: Stop feeding last of breakfast to ruminants (5)

indicatorNotes.feeding: the letter goes into the animals, as food would
indicatorNotes.last of: the last of anything is its end, so the last of a word is its final letter

annotation.surface: An order to stop giving leftover breakfast to the cows.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop feeding' looks like one instruction, but 'Stop' is the definition and 'feeding' the container signal.
annotation.definitionFit: To deter someone is to stop them doing something.

entries.clue: Frothy stuff Canadian native discussed? (6)

indicatorNotes.discussed: talked about, so it is the sound that counts

blocks.note: the moose is native to Canada

annotation.surface: People talk about some foamy substance made by an indigenous Canadian.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Canadian native' reads as a person; it is an animal.
annotation.definitionFit: Mousse is a light, frothy dessert or hair product.

entries.clue: Five coming inside, one figure out (5)

indicatorNotes.coming inside: the V enters the other word

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five

annotation.surface: Five people come indoors and one person comes out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One figure out' looks like a count of people; the definition is the phrasal verb 'figure out'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: working out the answer to a puzzle, as the solver is doing now.

entries.clue: Patient stuck in clinic, as expected (4)

indicatorNotes.stuck in: the answer is lodged inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: A patient is kept waiting at the clinic, as you would expect.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Patient' is a noun here, not the virtue of waiting.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical usage: doctors speak of the person they treat as an instance of the illness.

entries.clue: What makes tennis match impossible for nine players (5)

blocks.note: think of the one piece of kit strung across the court, and its absence

annotation.surface: Something that ruins a tennis match for nine players.
annotation.walkthrough: Tennis needs a net, so NO NET makes a match impossible. 'Players' suggests sport, but here they play instruments.
annotation.definitionFit: A musical term: the nine-player counterpart of a quartet or octet.

entries.clue: Pulse felt with old age, not having died, surprisingly! (9)

indicatorNotes.not having: the age is described as not having died, so that letter must be absent from it
indicatorNotes.surprisingly: the letters end up in an unexpected order

blocks.note: d = died, removed from OLD AGE

annotation.surface: A doctor takes a pulse and is surprised the old patient is still alive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks medical, but it is the edible seed: beans and lentils are pulses.
annotation.definitionFit: The flageolet is a small pale green French bean, a pulse.

entries.clue: Novel where honest scientist has released upright character? (12)

indicatorNotes.has released: the scientist lets go of a letter

blocks.note: I is the letter that stands straight up

annotation.surface: A novel in which an honest scientist sets free an upright creature.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface nods to the novel's plot, where a scientist releases his creature; the first I goes from EINSTEIN.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by title: Mary Shelley's 1818 Gothic novel about a scientist who builds a creature.
